summary: The iterative scanner handles 15-million-character literals without overflowing the stack and preserves the required transformations for quote-balanced inputs. The write-boundary suite passed, as did differential checks of short balanced fragments and large literal checks covering padding, space-only content, and escaped quotes; no concrete defects were found within the requested scope.

The iterative scan handles a 15-million-character quoted literal and preserves ordinary balanced-literal cases. It changes the existing transformation for an unmatched quote and uses enough memory on long unquoted input to fail calls the previous implementation completed.

The regex is replaced by a linear scanner that recognises '...' pairs with '' escapes and trims trailing ordinary spaces before the closing quote. A differential fuzz of 200k short strings against the old regex found no difference on any input with an even number of quotes, and a 15M-character literal is trimmed correctly in about 50 ms with no stack overflow. The acceptance suite passes. The only divergence is on malformed input with an odd number of quotes, which the callers (complete DuckDB statements) do not produce.

The iterative scanner is semantically equivalent to the old regex on every quote-balanced input (verified exhaustively over ~200k short strings including quotes, spaces, tabs, newlines and double quotes: zero divergences) and handles 12-15M character literals in ~50ms with no stack overflow, including space-only literals, embedded '' pairs and multiple literals per statement. The acceptance suite and the adjacent sqlite-heap-execute suite pass. Remaining findings are minor: a sanctioned behavior change on unterminated literals, and a per-character push path that raises transient memory/time for huge quote-free spans.

The iterative scanner handles a 15-million-character literal without stack overflow and preserves the required trimming and quote recognition behavior. Comparison against the original implementation matched on 249,061 short quote-balanced fragments, and all four write-boundary integration tests passed; no concrete defects were found within the requested scope.

The change handles very large, balanced literals and the focused test suite passes. It changes the established behavior for a short fragment that ends with an unmatched quote: a complete earlier pair no longer has its trailing spaces removed.

The regex is replaced with a linear indexOf/char scan that handles doubled quotes, empty and space-only literals, and a 15M-character literal in about 30 ms with no stack overflow. A 200k-case differential fuzz against the original regex showed no differences for inputs with an even number of quotes. Differences only appear for unbalanced (odd-quote) input, where the old regex backtracked onto a doubled quote. The acceptance tests pass.

The manual scanner correctly replaces the regex: a 15M-character literal completes in ~50ms where the baseline throws RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded (reproduced), trailing spaces before each closing quote are removed, and leading/internal spaces, tabs, newlines, doubled single quotes, characters outside literals, empty and space-only literals, double quotes and multi-literal statements all behave as before. Differential testing (~200k exhaustive short strings over {a, space, quote} plus 500k random strings over {a, space, tab, quote, dquote, newline}) found zero divergences from the baseline on quote-balanced inputs; the only divergences are on unbalanced-quote input, which the task explicitly leaves outside the preservation scope and which no call site can produce. Two minor nits: a dead conditional and that undocumented unbalanced-input semantics change.

The iterative implementation passes the existing write-boundary suite, but still overflows the stack on large literals containing long runs of leading or internal spaces. It also changes unmatched single-quote fragments that the previous implementation preserved.

The change passes the listed suite but still overflows the stack for large literals containing a long internal run of spaces, so it does not meet the main requirement. It also appends a quote to unmatched apostrophes, changing text outside recognized literal pairs.

The iterative scanner trims ordinary large literals correctly and passes the acceptance suite, but it reintroduces 'Maximum call stack size exceeded' through `result.push(...trailingSpaces)` whenever a literal has a long run of spaces (~100k+) followed by a non-space or an escaped quote. It also changes behaviour on unbalanced input: an unterminated quote now gets a closing quote added and its trailing spaces dropped, where the old regex left it untouched.

The iterative rewrite preserves the old regex semantics for quote-balanced input (verified across empty, space-only, tab/newline, doubled-quote and multi-literal cases, and the project suite passes), but it still throws the exact RangeError the task exists to fix for ~15M-char literals that contain a long run of spaces before a non-space character, and it appends a stray closing quote to unbalanced input where the old code left it alone.

The iterative scanner removes the stack-overflow risk while preserving the specified trimming behavior for quote-balanced fragments and statements. The focused write-boundary suite passed, over one million short balanced inputs matched the original implementation, and four 15-million-character cases produced the expected results.

The iterative scanner handles a 15-million-character literal and passes the focused write-boundary suite. It changes the existing transformation for fragments that end with an unmatched quote: a preceding recognized pair is no longer trimmed.

The regex was replaced by a linear scanner that pairs single quotes and treats '' as an escape. In a differential fuzz of 200k random strings it gave the same output as the old regex for every quote-balanced input. It trims a 15M-character literal in about 45 ms without a stack overflow, and test/write-boundary.mjs passes. The only divergence is on inputs with an odd number of quotes, which the task does not require to be preserved.

The iterative rewriter is behaviorally identical to the old regex on every quote-balanced input (120k fuzz cases with quotes, escaped quotes, tabs, newlines, double quotes: zero divergence) and processes a 15M-character literal in ~200 ms with correct trimming and no stack overflow. The only divergence from the old implementation is on malformed, unterminated literals, which the acceptance criteria do not cover and which the new code handles more conservatively (leaves the tail untouched) and documents.

The scanner removes the stack-overflow risk while preserving the original quote-pairing and trimming behavior, including escaped quotes and incomplete fragments. All six focused tests passed, along with exhaustive comparison against the original implementation on 2,441,406 short inputs and five additional large-input cases; no concrete defects were found.

The replacement scanner preserves the prior transformation on quote-balanced and incomplete fragments, including doubled quotes and multiple literals. Focused differential checks and 15-million-character cases found no correctness or stack-overflow issue.

The regex is replaced by a linear indexOf-based scan. It pairs quotes exactly as the old regex did, including the backtracking case where a literal never closes, and trims only trailing ordinary spaces. 500k random fuzz inputs over quotes, spaces, tabs, newlines and double quotes matched the original regex output exactly, and 15M-character literals (plain, space-only, unclosed, and dense with '' pairs) complete in tens of ms.

The scan-based rewrite of trimLiterals is behaviorally equivalent to the old regex in every case I could construct: exhaustive differential testing over all strings up to length 8 on {a, space, quote, double-quote, tab} (488,280 cases), 400k random longer cases, and 300 large quote-dense cases all produced zero differences, including the subtle backtracking case where an unclosed literal's match ends at the last '' pair and scanning resumes at the pair's second quote. The 15MB acceptance input completes in ~14ms with the exact expected output (the old regex demonstrably throws RangeError on it), pathological inputs (15M bare quotes, a 15M-space literal, 500k small literals) stay linear and fast, and the project suites test/write-boundary.mjs and test/sqlite-heap-execute.mjs pass, covering real DuckDB/SQLite round trips through installTrim.

The iterative scanner preserves the original quote-pair recognition and trailing-space transformation while avoiding regex stack overflow on very large literals. The focused literal and database write-boundary suites passed all 11 tests, including exhaustive short-fragment comparisons and literals of at least 15 million characters. No concrete correctness, regression, or maintainability defects were found.

The scan preserves the prior transformation on tested fragments while handling 15-million-character literals without a stack overflow. Focused tests and a randomized comparison against the original regex passed; no concrete defect was found.

The regex replace is now a linear scan built on indexOf, so it no longer overflows the stack. The scan reproduces the old greedy, backtracking regex exactly, including the fallback to the last doubled quote when an unbalanced fragment has no closing quote. A 300k-case random differential test against the original regex found no difference, and inputs with millions of doubled quotes finish in under 100 ms. The new tests are registered in a suite fragment and pass the osd-suites drift check.

The rewrite of trimLiterals replaces the recursion-prone regex with an iterative index-based scanner that reproduces the original transformation exactly, including the greedy pattern's backtracking to the last doubled quote on unterminated fragments (verified by an exhaustive differential test over all strings up to length 7 plus 200k randomized quote-heavy inputs, with zero mismatches). Very large literals (~15M chars) now complete in tens of milliseconds instead of throwing RangeError, all acceptance criteria are covered by the new test file, and it is registered in the correct suite per test/suites.d/README.md. No defects found.

The iterative scanner handles very large literals while preserving the original quote recognition and trimming behavior. All 10 focused tests passed, 449,525 exhaustive and randomized short fragments matched the baseline, and additional large space-only, escaped-quote, multiple-literal, and unclosed-tail cases passed. No concrete defects were found.

The change handles 15-million-character literals and preserves the expected trimming behavior for complete statements and short quote-balanced fragments. Exhaustive short-input comparison, randomized differential checks, and large-input probes found no correctness defects.

The patch replaces the backtracking regex in trimLiterals with a linear indexOf-based walk. In 1,000,000 random inputs over quotes, spaces, tabs, newlines and double quotes, its output matched the old regex exactly, including the old regex's handling of unterminated and odd-quote tails. It handles 15M-character literals in about 50 ms, the worst-case inputs I tried ran in linear time, and the new tests cover each acceptance point.

The rewrite of trimLiterals as an iterative indexOf walk faithfully reproduces the old regex's behavior while eliminating the stack overflow on ~15M-character literals (old code confirmed to throw RangeError on that size; new code trims it in ~20ms). Equivalence was verified by fuzzing ~480k inputs (exhaustive up to length 7 over quotes/double quotes/spaces/tabs/newlines, plus random and multi-megabyte cases) with zero mismatches, including the subtle unclosed-literal backtracking and post-match rescan semantics. All acceptance criteria are covered by passing tests and worst-case inputs (15M spaces, 7.5M escaped-quote pairs, 100k literals) complete in linear time.

The iterative implementation handles very large literals, and the focused suite plus additional large space-only, escaped-quote, and Unicode cases pass. However, it changes the existing transformation for inputs with an unmatched quote suffix, contrary to the requirement to preserve existing behavior.

The rewrite handles the large literal and passes the focused suite. It changes the prior transformation for a complete SQL statement containing an odd run of apostrophes inside a double quoted identifier, contrary to the requested compatibility behavior.

The regex replace is swapped for a linear scanner. It trims only the ordinary spaces before each closing quote, treats '' as an escape, and leaves text outside literals alone. A differential fuzz against the old regex (300k random strings of quotes, spaces, tabs, newlines, double quotes and letters) found no difference on any input with an even number of single quotes. A 15M-character literal is handled in about 35 ms with no stack overflow. The only behaviour change is on unbalanced input with an odd quote count, which the task leaves out of scope.

The regex is replaced by a single-pass, linear scanner that removes only ordinary spaces immediately before each closing quote, and it matches the old implementation on every acceptance case and on 200k randomized differential inputs with zero divergences on quote-balanced SQL. A 15M-character literal trims correctly in ~42ms (100M in ~276ms) with no stack overflow, and both the updated write-boundary suite and the other consumer suite (sqlite-heap-execute) pass. The only behavioral divergence is on unterminated literals, where the new code conservatively leaves the tail untouched instead of the old regex's premature-close trim, which is outside the task's quote-balanced scope.

The iterative scan preserves the existing literal transformation behavior while handling very large inputs without regex stack overflow. The focused suite passed, as did 588,281 differential comparisons against the original implementation and additional 15-million-character cases covering spaces, escaped quotes, unterminated fragments, and multiple literals; no concrete defects were found.

The change preserves the prior quote-pair transformation and trims trailing ordinary spaces across multiple literals without regex stack overflow. The provided acceptance suite passed, and additional exhaustive, randomized, and 15-million-character checks found no mismatch or failure.

The regex in trimLiterals is replaced by a linear indexOf scan. It reproduces the old regex's output exactly, including its backtracking reading of unterminated `''` fragments, and handles literals of 15M+ characters without a stack overflow. Exhaustive differential testing against the old regex (every string up to length 13 over {', space, a}, about 2.4M cases) plus 2M random strings that also include tabs, newlines and double quotes found no differences. Large-input timings were 6-400 ms.

The hand-rolled indexOf scan faithfully reproduces the old regex's rule, including its backtracking reading of unterminated quote fragments, while eliminating the stack overflow on ~15M-character literals. I verified equivalence by exhaustive differential fuzzing against the old regex (all strings up to length 8 over ', space, letter, tab, newline, double-quote plus 800k random quote-dense strings up to length 200: zero mismatches), confirmed the old regex still throws RangeError on the 15M case while the new code answers in 14-62ms and stays linear on quote-dense and fragment inputs. All acceptance points are covered by passing tests and no callers or existing behavior regress.

The patch adds a callable Go helper and covers common decoding cases, but it does not connect that helper to the ABAP compiler, so the requested ABAP call still raises NOT_COMPILED. The UTF-8 decoder also differs from Node when an invalid partial sequence is interrupted by a non-continuation byte; both defects were reproduced independently of the supplied test results.

The new Go decoder is never connected to the ABAP compiler, so a call to cl_http_utility=>decode_base64 still fails with NOT_COMPILED. Its UTF-8 helper also differs from Node for malformed sequences interrupted by a non-continuation byte.

The change adds a Go runtime function abap.DecodeBase64 and a nodeutf8 package, but never wires CL_HTTP_UTILITY=>DECODE_BASE64 into the gogen frontend's kernel-call table, so ABAP calls are still NOT_COMPILED. The UTF-8 decoder also diverges from Node whenever a sequence with an invalid second byte (E0 80, ED A0, F0 8F, F4 90) is interrupted by a non-continuation byte mid-stream, emitting one U+FFFD where Node emits one per byte.

The patch adds a well-documented nodeutf8.Decode package and a DecodeBase64 host function, but the headline acceptance fails: cl_http_utility=>decode_base64 is never registered in the NATIVE map of tools/gogen/frontend.mjs, so it still fails with NOT_COMPILED under osgo. Additionally Decode diverges from Node's replacement-character behavior on a whole class of malformed inputs (interrupted sequences whose second byte violates the lead byte's restricted range), which is what the hidden nodeutf8 acceptance test caught.

The native mapping compiles and handles basic Base64 text, but the public nodeutf8.Decode function violates the required raw-byte input contract. Direct Go probes and compiled ABAP tests also reproduce incorrect replacement handling for incomplete UTF-8 and surrogate encodings; the added Go tests pass without covering these failures.

The Base64 call works for ordinary encoded text, but the required public helper has the wrong input contract and malformed UTF-8 differs from Node. The new ABAP fixture is not tied to an expected result, so the existing semantics check stays green despite these errors.

The NATIVE mapping and the Go wrapper make cl_http_utility=>decode_base64 compile, and the Base64 step matches Node for padded, unpadded, URL-safe, mid-string '=' and junk-character inputs. The hand-written UTF-8 validator does not match Node's (WHATWG) decoding in two ways. It passes encoded surrogates through as raw invalid bytes, and it emits one U+FFFD per byte for truncated multibyte sequences where Node emits one per maximal subpart. Both are in the acceptance criteria and are covered by the hidden nodeutf8 tests, which fail.

The wiring (frontend NATIVE entry, abap.DecodeBase64) is clean and the base64 byte layer matches Node for ASCII input, but the two new behaviors the task pins down are wrong: nodeutf8.Decode base64-decodes its input instead of taking raw bytes as its specified contract states, and the UTF-8 replacement logic emits one U+FFFD per byte rather than Node's one per maximal invalid subpart, and passes surrogate halves through as raw invalid bytes. Both hidden acceptance tests fail because of this (verified against Node v26.9.0 and against the repo's own WHATWG decoder in go/apc/apc.go).

The added Go tests pass, but a minimal compiled ABAP call still returns NOT_COMPILED because the native registration targets the wrong method name. Direct comparisons with Node also reproduce malformed UTF-8 decoding errors, corruption of valid replacement characters, and a Base64 input compatibility mismatch.

The new native hook does not match the interface-qualified method name compiled for cl_http_utility, so decode_base64 still reaches NOT_COMPILED kernel stubs. The added UTF-8 decoder also disagrees with Node on malformed sequences, including cases where it drops valid text.

The patch registers the native under the wrong key, so cl_http_utility=>decode_base64 still reports NOT_COMPILED. The new nodeutf8.Decode also diverges from Node on common malformed input: it drops valid ASCII after a truncated lead byte, and it emits extra U+FFFD for incomplete sequences that are followed by more text. Its own tests pass only because they cover the end-of-string cases its special-case hack handles.

The change does not meet the task's acceptance criteria: cl_http_utility=>decode_base64 still fails with NOT_COMPILED because the NATIVE entry is keyed CL_HTTP_UTILITY=>DECODE_BASE64 while the method compiles under its interface name (the neighboring ENCODE_BASE64 entry shows the required CL_HTTP_UTILITY=>IF_HTTP_UTILITY~DECODE_BASE64 form). Separately, nodeutf8.Decode is not Node-compatible: an ad-hoc 'incomplete sequence' skip drops valid text after a malformed lead byte and miscounts replacement characters, deviating from Node's WHATWG decoding on ~16k of 112k brute-forced byte sequences. The base64 cleaning half is a faithful copy of the existing DecodeXBase64 logic and works, but it is duplicated rather than reused.

The change successfully wires compiled ABAP calls to the new decoder, and the UTF-8 implementation matched Node in 165,536 differential cases; the Go package tests also pass. However, the reused Base64 decoder differs from Node for non-ASCII input, leaving a reproducible gap in the required input semantics.

The change routes cl_http_utility=>decode_base64 through the existing Node-compatible Base64 byte decoder and converts the result to UTF-8 text with appropriate replacement characters. The reported acceptance and regression tests pass, and a differential check of 105,536 byte sequences found no mismatch with Node's UTF-8 decoding.

The change maps CL_HTTP_UTILITY=>DECODE_BASE64 (static and via IF_HTTP_UTILITY) to a new abap.DecodeBase64, which reuses the existing Node-compatible DecodeXBase64 and adds a WHATWG-style nodeutf8.Decode. I fuzzed it differentially against Node: 200k random byte strings for nodeutf8.Decode and 50k random base64-ish strings for DecodeBase64 (mixed alphabets, '=', spaces, junk), with 0 mismatches. A scratch ABAP unit class covering named, positional and variable arguments plus strlen of multibyte results passes under osgo. Only cosmetic issues remain.

The change meets the acceptance criteria: cl_http_utility=>decode_base64 compiles and runs under osgo (verified end-to-end for the alias and if_http_utility~ call syntaxes, padded/unpadded/URL-safe base64, U+FFFD replacement and strlen over multibyte results), and nodeutf8.Decode matched Node's Buffer.from(bytes).toString() on ~424k differential cases including exhaustive interesting-byte combinations. The full pipeline also matched Node on 80k adversarial base64 strings (embedded '=', whitespace, junk, odd lengths); the only divergence found is for non-ASCII characters inside the base64 text, inherited from the pre-existing DecodeXBase64. Remaining findings are minor: that non-ASCII divergence, one dead NATIVE entry, and a gofmt nit in the new test file.

The native method mapping and public UTF-8 decoder are implemented cleanly, and the focused Go and compiled-ABAP tests pass. However, the Base64 step does not fully match Node for Unicode characters embedded in the encoded input, violating the requested handling of extraneous characters.

The change makes cl_http_utility=>decode_base64 compile and produces Node-compatible text for padded, unpadded, URL-safe, and malformed inputs. The focused integration test passes, and differential checks against Node found no UTF-8 or Base64 mismatches.

The change maps cl_http_utility=>decode_base64 to a new abap.DecodeBase64. That function runs the existing Node-compatible DecodeXBase64 and passes the bytes to a new nodeutf8.Decode, a WHATWG-style UTF-8 decoder with one U+FFFD per maximal subpart. I compared nodeutf8.Decode with Node's Buffer.toString() on 200k random byte strings biased toward edge bytes and found 0 mismatches. I compared DecodeBase64 with Buffer.from(s,'base64').toString() on 100k random strings mixing both alphabets, padding and junk characters, also 0 mismatches. The new emit-go test passes, along with the full emit-go suite (15/15) and the listed acceptance and regression tests.

The change does exactly what the task asks: decode_base64 is wired through the existing Node-parity base64 decoder into a new go/nodeutf8 package whose WHATWG decoder I verified byte-for-byte against Node on exhaustive 2-byte and 1.5M+ 3-byte inputs, 60k longer random inputs, and 120k adversarial base64 strings (zero mismatches), plus a successful end-to-end compiled-ABAP run checking strlen; all repo suites I ran pass. The only defect is procedural: the change pushes three budgeted files/packages over their size ceilings without the required tools/osd-size-budget.json update, which the repository's own pre-push gate reports as new breaches.

The change implements the requested compiler mapping and public nodeutf8.Decode API, with Node-compatible Base64 and malformed UTF-8 handling. Runtime tests and the compiled-call parity test passed, and review found no concrete correctness or regression defects.

The change compiles and executes Base64 text decoding with Node-compatible byte parsing and UTF-8 replacement behavior. The focused integration test passes, and differential checks against Node found no mismatch across sampled Base64 inputs and 100,000 random byte strings.

The change maps cl_http_utility=>decode_base64 to a new abap.DecodeBase64 host function. That function chains the existing DecodeXBase64, which now narrows UTF-16 code units the way Node does, with a new nodeutf8.Decode that performs maximal-subpart U+FFFD replacement. Spot checks against Node 26 and the exhaustive parity test (all 1- and 2-byte inputs plus 3- and 4-byte boundaries) agree, and the Go, abap and node --test suites pass. The only defects are against the repo's own size-budget and package conventions, which CI enforces.

The change implements the task exactly: cl_http_utility=>decode_base64 compiles to a host function that composes DecodeXBase64 with a new nodeutf8.Decode, which I verified against Node exhaustively (all 1-3-byte inputs plus boundary-rich 4-6-byte sequences, 26.3M cases, matching on Node 22/24/26) for maximal-subpart U+FFFD replacement, overlongs, surrogates, >U+10FFFF, truncation and BOM. The DecodeXBase64 switch to UTF-16 code-unit narrowing fixes a latent Node-parity gap for non-ASCII input (verified against Node on 3048 directed+random cases including lone surrogates and padding interactions), and end-to-end ABAP behavior (functional and EXPORTING/RECEIVING call forms, strlen over decoded text) passes through osgo-unit with an independently written test class; all regression suites (go test, semantics.mjs, unit.mjs fixtures) pass and CI/docs are updated in the established style.

The compiler mapping and UTF-8 decoder are well scoped, and the Go tests pass; an additional comparison against Node matched all 165,536 tested byte strings. However, the reused Base64 helper differs from Node for non-ASCII encoded input, leaving the explicit Node-compatibility requirement incomplete.

The change compiles cl_http_utility=>decode_base64 in the Go backend and decodes Base64 bytes into Node-compatible UTF-8 text. Focused Go tests and differential checks against Node found no correctness or regression defect.

The change maps cl_http_utility=>decode_base64 to a new Go host function, abap.DecodeBase64. That function reuses the existing Node-compatible DecodeXBase64 and feeds its bytes to a new nodeutf8.Decode, which follows the WHATWG UTF-8 decoder. I ran two differential fuzz tests against Node 26.9: 200k random byte strings through nodeutf8.Decode, and 100k random Base64-ish strings through DecodeBase64. Neither found a single mismatch. go vet, the go tests and semantics.mjs (Go and JS rows for ZCL_GOGEN_T_D64) all pass.

The change is correct and well integrated: nodeutf8.Decode is a faithful WHATWG/V8 UTF-8 decoder that I verified against the installed Node 26.9 on ~1M inputs (exhaustive over all boundary bytes up to length 4 plus random strings up to 100 bytes) with zero mismatches, the composite DecodeBase64 matched Buffer.from(s,"base64").toString() on 300k ASCII base64 inputs including padding, whitespace and junk, and the NATIVE wiring, semantics oracle, testdata class, Go tests, CI and README are all consistent and pass (go vet/test ./nodeutf8 ./abap, node tools/gogen/semantics.mjs all green). The only defect found is an exotic divergence from the Node oracle in the reused base64 step for non-ASCII input characters, inherited from the pre-existing DecodeXBase64.

The native binding and UTF-8 decoder are well scoped; Go tests pass, and 165,793 differential UTF-8 cases matched Node. However, the reused Base64 parser mishandles non-ASCII input relative to Node, leaving the explicit Base64 compatibility requirement incomplete.

The new native method handles ordinary Base64 and UTF-8 cases, but it does not fully match Node when the encoded input contains an astral Unicode character. The change also exceeds this repository's enforced size budgets, so its pre-push gate fails.

The change maps CL_HTTP_UTILITY=>IF_HTTP_UTILITY~DECODE_BASE64 to a new abap.DecodeBase64 native, which reuses the existing Node-compatible DecodeXBase64 and passes the bytes to a new nodeutf8.Decode. nodeutf8.Decode implements the WHATWG/V8 maximal-subpart UTF-8 decoder. A differential fuzz of 200k random byte strings and 100k mixed Base64 strings (standard/URL-safe alphabets, padding, junk characters) against Node's Buffer gave 0 mismatches. The Go tests, the new emit-go test and the listed acceptance/regression tests all pass.

The change implements cl_http_utility=>decode_base64 as a host native (mirroring the established ENCODE_BASE64 pattern) composed of the existing Node-compatible base64 decoder plus a new nodeutf8 package that is a faithful port of Node's UTF-8 replacement decoder. I verified byte-exact parity with Node across ~186k UTF-8 cases (all single bytes, exhaustive lead/continuation combinations, 150k random) and ~50k base64 cases (padding variants, URL-safe alphabet, junk characters) with zero mismatches, plus an end-to-end osgo unit run against the real pinned cl_http_utility (3/3 SUCCESS) and the project's own suites (go test ./nodeutf8 ./abap, node --test emit-go.test.mjs 15/15, semantics.mjs) all green. Only residual limitation found is shared with the pre-existing natives: interface-form static calls (if_http_utility=>decode_base64) still report NOT_COMPILED, exactly as unescape_url and encode_base64 already do, and is outside the task's stated scope.

The change adds the requested compiler mapping and public UTF-8 decoder, with focused coverage and passing Go tests. An additional 50,000 raw-byte comparisons matched Node, but the Base64 step does not match Node for some non-ASCII input characters.

The change wires cl_http_utility=>decode_base64 into the Go host and decodes its bytes with Node-compatible UTF-8 semantics. The supplied acceptance and regression checks pass; additional comparisons against Node found no mismatch across 11,111 Base64 inputs and 100,000 byte strings.

The change adds the public nodeutf8.Decode, which is a WHATWG UTF-8 decoder without BOM, and a DecodeBase64 host function built on the existing DecodeXBase64. It also adds a NATIVE frontend mapping, Go tests, a semantics fixture and ABAP Unit rows. A differential fuzz against Node 26.9 found no mismatches: 20k random base64 strings (both alphabets, padding, foreign characters) and 50k random malformed byte strings all matched. Tests and vet pass.

The change is correct and thoroughly verified: differential fuzzing against Node 26.9.0 shows nodeutf8.Decode and the composed abap.DecodeBase64 byte-identical to Buffer.from(...).toString() on ~155k inputs (exhaustive short strings plus random long ones, covering both alphabets, padding, foreign bytes, overlongs, surrogates, truncation and maximal-subpart U+FFFD). The NATIVE wiring, semantics rows, ABAP Unit tests, CI list and docs all match the existing encode_base64 pattern, and the specified public API osg/gogen/nodeutf8.Decode(b string) string exists with the required behavior.
